lines.text: Congress required an appropriate medical screening in emergency rooms. The court immediately faced a problem: the statute never explained what appropriate actually meant.
The opinion called appropriate one of the most wonderful weasel words in the dictionary, useful because nobody publicly argues for inappropriate treatment.
But the joke did not decide the case. The court still needed a legal test that hospitals and patients could understand.
Its answer began with a real screening procedure reasonably designed to identify critical conditions in people who arrive with symptoms.
Then came the controlling comparison: patients presenting substantially similar complaints must receive that level of screening uniformly.
The essence, the court said, is that some procedure exists and that the hospital administers it even-handedly.
That does not turn federal law into a promise of excellent medicine. A hospital can examine everyone badly without violating this particular rule.
So appropriate was not defined as best. It was defined through procedure and sameness, returning us to the slippery word that opened the case.
